Acetic acid with sodium acetate is an acidic buffer, so use the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation:
pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid])
The ratio [salt]/[acid] is increased **ten times**, so the new pH is
pH(new) = pKa + log(10 × [salt]/[acid])
= pKa + log 10 + log([salt]/[acid])
= pH(old) + 1
The logarithm is what tames the change: multiplying the ratio by ten adds just **one** unit to
the pH, it does not multiply the pH by ten.
That is exactly why options (1) and (2) are wrong — pH is already a logarithmic quantity, so
it shifts additively.
The pH **rises** because more salt means more of the conjugate base, making the solution less
acidic, which rules out (4).
∴ it increases by one.

kcet|Chemistry|2004|38||0|0.s:
This is the controlled catalytic oxidation of methane, and the catalyst is chosen to stop the
oxidation at the first stage.
CH₄ + O₂ --Mo₂O₃, 700 K--> HCHO + H₂O
The product is **methanal** (formaldehyde) ✓
Without the catalyst, methane simply burns all the way to CO₂ and H₂O. Molybdenum oxide
holds the oxidation at the aldehyde.
Note the sequence of oxidation states of the carbon: methane ⇒ methanol ⇒ methanal ⇒
methanoic acid ⇒ CO₂. Different catalysts stop it at different points — Cu at 523 K and high
pressure gives methanol instead, which is where option (1) comes from.
Ethanal (4) is impossible here, since methane has only one carbon and none is added.
∴ methanal.

kcet|Chemistry|2004|39||0|0.s:
Two different routes to benzene, each needing its own reagent.
**From benzoic acid** — decarboxylation. Heating the acid with **soda lime** (NaOH + CaO)
removes the –COOH as carbonate:
C₆H₅COOH + NaOH --CaO, Δ--> C₆H₆ + Na₂CO₃
So X = soda lime.
**From phenol** — reduction. Distilling phenol with **zinc dust** removes the oxygen:
C₆H₅OH + Zn ⇒ C₆H₆ + ZnO
So Y = zinc dust.
The question asks for X and Y in that order, so the answer must read soda lime first and zinc
dust second ✓
Option (3) has them the right pair but the wrong way round, which is the trap. Soda lime
cannot reduce phenol, and zinc dust cannot decarboxylate an acid.
∴ soda lime and zinc dust.

kcet|Chemistry|2004|40||0|0.s:
Boiling with alcoholic potash hydrolyses an **ester** into the potassium salt of its acid plus
an alcohol:
RCOOR′ + KOH ⇒ RCOOK + R′OH
Acidifying then liberates the free acid:
RCOOK + HCl ⇒ RCOOH + KCl
The clue is that the acid separates as a **white solid**, so it must be insoluble in water.
Check the four:
(1) ethyl acetate and (2) methyl acetate both give acetic acid — completely miscible with
water, so nothing separates.
(4) ethyl formate gives formic acid — again fully miscible.
(3) ethyl benzoate gives **benzoic acid**, which is only sparingly soluble in cold water
(about 3 g per litre) and crystallises out as a white solid ✓
That insolubility is the whole point of the observation, and is how benzoic acid is isolated in
practice.
∴ ethyl benzoate.

kcet|Chemistry|2004|41||0|0.s:
H₂S is a weak acid and ionises only slightly:
H₂S ⇌ 2H⁺ + S²⁻
Dilute HCl is a strong acid and floods the solution with H⁺. By Le Chatelier that common ion
pushes the equilibrium **to the left**, suppressing the ionisation of H₂S and keeping the
sulphide ion concentration very low.
That is precisely what is wanted. Group II cations (Cu²⁺, Pb²⁺, Bi³⁺, Cd²⁺) form sulphides
with extremely small Ksp, so even this tiny [S²⁻] is enough to exceed it and they precipitate.
Group IV cations (Zn²⁺, Mn²⁺, Co²⁺, Ni²⁺) have much larger Ksp values, so they stay in solution.
Without the acid, [S²⁻] would be high enough to precipitate both groups together and the
separation would fail.
Group IV is then precipitated later by making the solution ammoniacal, which raises [S²⁻] again.
∴ to decrease the dissociation of H₂S.

kcet|Chemistry|2004|42||0|0.s:
Aluminium displaces hydrogen from acid but silver does not, so aluminium is the more reactive
metal — it is **oxidised** and acts as the anode, while silver is the cathode.
E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode
2.46 = 0.80 − E°(Al³⁺/Al)
E°(Al³⁺/Al) = 0.80 − 2.46
E°(Al³⁺/Al) = **−1.66 V**
The negative value is the check that the answer is sensible: a metal that displaces hydrogen
must have a reduction potential below that of hydrogen, which is 0.00 V by definition.
Option (3), +1.66 V, is the same figure with the electrodes assigned the wrong way round.
Note also that the potential is **not** multiplied by 3 for the three electrons — electrode
potential is an intensive property and does not scale with n, even though ΔG° does.
∴ −1.66 V.

kcet|Chemistry|2004|43||0|0:
Fractional distillation separates petroleum by boiling point: whatever boils lowest comes off
first, at the top of the column.
The fractions in order of increasing boiling point are:
**Uncondensed hydrocarbon gases** — C₁ to C₄, below 20 °C ← the first fraction off
Gasoline or petrol — C₅ to C₁₀, 40–180 °C
Kerosene — C₁₀ to C₁₆, 180–250 °C
Diesel oil — C₁₅ to C₁₈, 250–320 °C
Lubricating oil, then the residue of bitumen
The gases are the smallest molecules, with the weakest van der Waals forces between them,
so they need the least energy to escape and emerge before anything else.
Gasoline (1) is a tempting answer because it is the most familiar product, but it is the second
fraction, not the first.
∴ hydrocarbon gases.
kcet|Chemistry|2004|44||0|0:
Bleaching powder, CaOCl₂, supplies chlorine in water, so this is the **haloform** reaction and
the product trichloromethane is chloroform, CHCl₃.
The reaction needs a CH₃–CO– group, or a CH₃–CH(OH)– group that the chlorine first oxidises
to one.
Ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, has exactly that CH₃–CH(OH)– unit:
first it is oxidised to ethanal, CH₃CHO
then the methyl is trichlorinated to CCl₃CHO
finally alkali cleaves it to CHCl₃ + HCOO⁻ ✓
Now the others:
(2) Methanol, CH₃OH — only one carbon, so no CH₃ next to the carbinol carbon.
(3) Methanal, HCHO — again one carbon, no methyl group.
(4) Phenol — the OH is on an aromatic ring with no adjacent CH₃; chlorine substitutes on the
ring instead.
∴ ethanol.
kcet|Chemistry|2004|45||0|0:
Benzoin is C₆H₅–CO–CH(OH)–C₆H₅, formed when two molecules of benzaldehyde couple in the
presence of cyanide — the benzoin condensation.
Look at the two functional groups in that structure:
a **ketone** carbonyl, C₆H₅–CO–
an **alcohol**, –CH(OH)–, on the carbon immediately next to it
A hydroxyl group on the carbon adjacent to a carbonyl is an **α-hydroxy** group, and since
the carbonyl here is a ketone, benzoin is an **α-hydroxy ketone** ✓
It is not an α-hydroxy aldehyde (1), because the carbonyl carbon carries a phenyl group, not
a hydrogen.
Option (3) is wrong for the same reason — there is no aldehyde present — and (4) describes
an unsaturated acid, which benzoin is not.
Oxidising benzoin gives benzil, the diketone, confirming that the OH sits next to a C=O.
∴ an α-hydroxy ketone.

kcet|Chemistry|2004|46||0|0.s:
Use the temperature coefficient rule: the rate constant roughly **doubles** for every 10 K rise.
Find the number of 10 K intervals:
n = (310 − 290)/10 = 20/10 = 2
Each interval doubles k, and the effect compounds:
k(310) = k(290) × 2ⁿ = 3.2 × 10⁻³ × 2²
= 3.2 × 10⁻³ × 4
= 1.28 × 10⁻² s⁻¹
So the reaction is four times as fast, not twice — the growth is exponential in the number of
intervals, which is why option (1), merely tripling, and option (3), doubling, are both wrong.
Option (4) has the constant **decreasing**, which would contradict Arrhenius: k always rises
with temperature.
∴ about 1.28 × 10⁻² s⁻¹.
